\chapter{Eyes, Ears, Mouth, and Nose}
\label{ch:russian-face-parts}
\hlchaptermodality{9}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the ear, nose, mouth and eye in Russian with their genders, and say which trace to a secure ancient root and which do not.}

The chapter closes on \ru{глаз}, the word that quietly evicted Russian's true inherited eye-word: the reader produces all four face words with their genders, names \ru{ухо} and \ru{нос} as secure PIE cognates, names \ru{рот} as an honest dead end, and traces \ru{глаз} back to slang for 'ball' while placing the real cousin of English eye, \ru{око}, inside \ru{очки}. It is the first realization of SPINE-CHECK-WELLBEING in this track, and it reaches back to Chapter 3's \ru{видеть} and \ru{говорить}, rescuing three atoms nothing had revisited.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[úkho]{\ru{ухо} — \textquotedblleft{}ear,\textquotedblright{} and Russian's third gender finally arrives}

\label{lesson:RU-C09-ukho}



\begin{quote}
A new chapter, a new part of the body, and the last of Chapter 6's three genders — held back until now, on purpose.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{ухо}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{ухо}} — \emph{úkho} — \textbf{ear}. \textbf{Neuter.}
\end{quote}

Stress on the first syllable: \emph{Ú-kho}. Ends in \textbf{-\ru{о}}, so — finally — Chapter 6's third row: \textbf{-\ru{о} and -\ru{е} mark the neuter}, and here is the first word in this book to actually wear it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{ухо}} is Indo-European *\emph{h\textsubscript{2}ous-}, and the cousin web is about as tight as this book gets: English \textbf{ear} is the same word; so is Latin \textbf{auris} ($\to$ \textbf{auricle}, \textbf{aural}), and Greek \textbf{ous} ($\to$ \textbf{otitis}, an ear infection). Four languages, one unbroken thread from a single ancient root — no borrowing, no replacement, nothing lost along the way.

That makes \emph{\ru{ухо}} the plainest kind of cousin in this book: not a loanword like \emph{\ru{кофе}}, not a word that replaced an older one, just the same PIE root worn down four different ways in four different mouths.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{ухо}\textquotedblright{} — stress on the front, neuter
  \item the third row — \textquotedblleft{}-\ru{о} and -\ru{е}, neuter\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ear, auris, ous\textquotedblright{} — one root, three languages
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}ear.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{\ru{Ухо}}.) What gender is it, and which ending finally shows it? (\textbf{Neuter} — \textbf{-\ru{о}}.) Name two other languages that share the same root word for \textquotedblleft{}ear.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{English \emph{ear}, Latin \emph{auris}} — also Greek \emph{ous}.) Is this word borrowed or inherited? (\textbf{Inherited}, straight from PIE, no detour.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nos]{\ru{нос} — \textquotedblleft{}nose,\textquotedblright{} a second straight cousin in a row}

\label{lesson:RU-C09-nos}



\begin{quote}
One syllable, one gender back to consonant-final masculine, and another word that never left the family.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{нос}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{нос}} — \emph{nos} — \textbf{nose}. \textbf{Masculine.}
\end{quote}

Consonant-final, back to the first row of Chapter 6's table. Every letter is one you have read since Chapter 1.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{нос}} is Indo-European *\emph{nas-}, and it barely needs translating: English \textbf{nose} is the same word, and so is Latin \textbf{nasus} ($\to$ \textbf{nasal}, \textbf{nasturtium}, the \textquotedblleft{}nose-twisting\textquotedblright{} flower). Say \emph{nos} next to \emph{nose} and \emph{nasus} and the family resemblance needs no explaining at all.

Two body-part words in a row, \emph{\ru{ухо}} and \emph{\ru{нос}}, and both are the same kind of cousin: no loan, no replacement, just the same ancient root, worn down along three different paths to the same meaning.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{нос}\textquotedblright{} — one syllable, masculine
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nose, nasus\textquotedblright{} — barely disguised
  \item the pair so far — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{ухо}, \ru{нос}\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}nose,\textquotedblright{} with its gender. (\textbf{\ru{Нос}} — \textbf{masculine}.) Name its two closest cousins. (\textbf{English \emph{nose}, Latin \emph{nasus}.}) What English flower name comes from the Latin cousin? (\emph{\textbf{Nasturtium}}.) Which earlier word in this chapter is the same kind of straight inheritance? (\textbf{\ru{Ухо}}, \textquotedblleft{}ear.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rot]{\ru{рот} — \textquotedblleft{}mouth,\textquotedblright{} where the cousin trail actually runs out}

\label{lesson:RU-C09-rot}



\begin{quote}
Two straight cousins in a row was good luck, not the rule. This one has no secure English relative at all — and it belongs to a verb you already own.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{рот}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{рот}} — \emph{rot} — \textbf{mouth}. \textbf{Masculine.}
\end{quote}

Consonant-final, masculine again. \emph{(On paper this romanizes exactly like the English word \textbf{rot} — another spelling coincidence, like }\ru{друг}\emph{/}drug\emph{, with no shared history at all.)}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{\ru{Ухо}} and \emph{\ru{нос}} both handed you a clean English cousin. \textbf{\ru{рот}} does not. Its Proto-Slavic ancestor \textbf{*r\ru{ъ}t\ru{ъ}} originally meant \textquotedblleft{}beak, snout\textquotedblright{} and is \textbf{probably} related to \textbf{\ru{рыть}}, \textquotedblleft{}to dig, to burrow\textquotedblright{} — the picture of an animal's snout rooting through the ground, later widened to any mouth, including yours. There is \textbf{no secure link to English \emph{mouth}} at all: English's word comes from an entirely separate Germanic root, \textbf{*munþaz}, with no shared ancestor here. Where Chapter 4's \emph{\ru{читать}} had no English descendant, this word has no English \emph{ancestor} in common — a different kind of dead end, and worth naming exactly that plainly rather than forcing a connection that isn't there.

What \emph{\ru{рот}} does have is a job you have been practising since Chapter 3: it is what makes \textbf{\ru{говорить}} possible. You met \textbf{\ru{г}} as Greek gamma on \emph{\ru{говорить}}'s very first line; here is the mouth that has been saying it ever since.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{рот}\textquotedblright{} — one syllable, masculine
  \item the honest dead end — \textquotedblleft{}no English cousin, only \ru{рыть}, 'to dig'\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{рот}, \ru{говорить}\textquotedblright{} — the mouth, and what it has been doing since Chapter 3
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}mouth,\textquotedblright{} with its gender. (\textbf{\ru{Рот}} — \textbf{masculine}.) Is it related to English \emph{mouth}? (\textbf{No} — separate Germanic root, no shared ancestor.) What is its own best guess of an origin? (\textbf{\ru{Рыть}}, \textquotedblleft{}to dig\textquotedblright{} — a snout rooting the ground.) Which Chapter 3 verb does the mouth make possible, and what letter did that verb first teach you? (\textbf{\ru{Говорить}}; the letter \textbf{\ru{г}}, Greek gamma.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[glaz]{\ru{глаз} — \textquotedblleft{}eye,\textquotedblright{} the word for the eye that isn't the word for the eye}

\label{lesson:RU-C09-glaz}



\begin{quote}
The last of four face words, and the strangest story in the chapter: Russian's everyday word for \textquotedblleft{}eye\textquotedblright{} is not the word Indo-European gave it for \textquotedblleft{}eye\textquotedblright{} at all.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{глаз}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{глаз}} — \emph{glaz} — \textbf{eye}. \textbf{Masculine.}
\end{quote}

Consonant-final, masculine, closing the chapter's four with the same pattern that opened it in Chapter 6.

\emph{(Tempting, on the page, to link this to English \textbf{glass} — the spellings even rhyme. Resist it: they trace to two different PIE roots and are not cousins. Its real story is stranger than that coincidence.)}

\begin{cousinweb}
Every other body word in this chapter kept its ancient Indo-European name. \emph{\ru{Глаз}} did not. \textbf{\ru{Глаз}} began in Old Russian as \textbf{*glaz\ru{ъ}}, \textquotedblleft{}a ball, a glass bead, a smooth round stone\textquotedblright{} — PIE *\emph{g(\textsuperscript{h})el-}, \textquotedblleft{}round.\textquotedblright{} Starting around the sixteenth century it spread as slang for \textquotedblleft{}eyeball,\textquotedblright{} then simply \textquotedblleft{}eye,\textquotedblright{} and it \textbf{completely displaced} the true inherited word.

That older word was \textbf{\ru{око}} (plural \textbf{\ru{очи}}) — PIE *\emph{h\textsubscript{3}ók\textsuperscript{w}s}, the actual, secure cousin of English \textbf{eye} itself, the same root behind Latin \textbf{oculus} ($\to$ \textbf{ocular}, \textbf{monocle}) and Greek \textbf{ophthalmós}. \emph{\ru{Око}} still exists, but only in poetry and set phrases now. Its one everyday survivor is hiding in plain sight: \textbf{\ru{очки}}, \textquotedblleft{}eyeglasses,\textquotedblright{} is built directly on \textbf{\ru{очи}} — literally \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}little eyes.\textquotedblright{}} So the word that means \emph{eye} in Russian today is a Slavic upstart; the word that is actually your cousin only shows up when you put spectacles on.

This is Chapter 3's \textbf{\ru{видеть}} completed at last: the organ that does the seeing turns out to have replaced its own name, while the verb for \emph{seeing} stayed put the whole time.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{глаз}\textquotedblright{} — masculine, and not related to English \emph{glass}
  \item the evicted word — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{око}, \ru{очи} — the real cousin of \emph{eye}\textquotedblright{}
  \item where it hides — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{очки}, 'little eyes'\textquotedblright{}
  \item the whole face — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{ухо}, \ru{нос}, \ru{рот}, \ru{глаз}\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}eye,\textquotedblright{} with its gender. (\textbf{\ru{Глаз}} — \textbf{masculine}.) What did \emph{\ru{глаз}} originally mean, and what word did it push out? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Round object, ball\textquotedblright{}}; it displaced \textbf{\ru{око}}.) Where does the true inherited eye-word survive today? (\textbf{\ru{Очки}}, \textquotedblleft{}glasses\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}little eyes.\textquotedblright{}) Name all four face words this chapter taught, in order. (\textbf{\ru{Ухо}, \ru{нос}, \ru{рот}, \ru{глаз}.}) Which Chapter 3 verb does the eye make possible, and what sound-swap did that verb teach in its \emph{I} form? (\textbf{\ru{Видеть}}; \textbf{\ru{д} $\to$ \ru{ж}}, as in \emph{\ru{вижу}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
